paras: The lynching of Billy Leroy and Sam Potter took place at Del Norte, Colorado, apparently on the night of May 22, 1881, when a party of men took the two captured stage robbers from the town jail and hanged them. Leroy, an escaped mail robber, and Potter had been brought to Del Norte as prisoners, and briefs printed across the country said they were lynched by citizens within an hour of arrival. A later account said a coroner's jury exonerated all concerned and that the dead men were brothers named Pond.

Leroy had been sentenced by Judge Hallett of the United States court to ten years in the penitentiary. He escaped from Deputy Marshal Cantril while being taken by train to the prison at Detroit. Coaches near Del Norte were then stopped and fired on; in one robbery three road agents wounded Frank Bartlett, a Denver and Rio Grande engineer, and took the mail sacks, and Del Norte citizens offered a reward.

A party of hunters guided by a tracker named Galloway went after the gang, and at dusk on the 22d they captured a man who surrendered when covered from three sides and admitted belonging to Le Roy's gang. On the road toward Alamosa they met a man with a pack who fired and ran; a hunter named Armstrong shot him in the calf, and once drawn out of the brush by the river he said he was Billy Le Roy. Del Norte was "crazy over the capture," and General R. A. Cameron said the streets were like hives of mad bees.

The sheriff locked the two prisoners in the rear cells of the jail, and a committee of citizens was appointed to guard them overnight. About ten o'clock the sheriff was seized and held in a room, and at eleven a party rode up, called the guards out as their "relief," and bound them one by one. The party took Le Roy and Potter from their cells, gagged them and left the jail without a word. At midnight a stranger told Coroner Holland that two men were hanging on a tree near the river, tossed him the jail keys and walked away, and the coroner cut down the bodies.

The next day the coroner's jury returned a verdict "exonerating all concerned in the affair." No report of arrests or a prosecution appears in the coverage. The narrative noted the initials "A. P." and "S. P." tattooed on the men's arms and gave their real names as Arthur and Samuel Pond, brothers.

Judge Bishop of Lake City sent his brother, a druggist, a photograph of the two bodies propped against the jail wall, one with a trouser leg rolled up to show the bullet wound. He wrote that the men had confessed before they were hanged and that the execution "much relieved the people of these parts."

News of the lynching first appeared as one-line wire items in weekly papers in Minnesota, Iowa, Wisconsin, New Jersey and Michigan from June 1. These items called the men "desperadoes," "notorious" or "Colorado murderers" and placed them among other crime briefs.

In Colorado, the Elk Mountain Pilot reprinted a Denver Republican paragraph on the "tragic end" of the stage robber that dwelt on Judge Hallett's sarcasm at his sentencing. The New York Sun turned the case into a moral tale of two Pennsylvania brothers who took up highway robbery until "public sentiment precipitated a disaster." Later in June a long narrative ran in the Grant County Herald in Dakota and the Centre Democrat of Bellefonte, Pennsylvania, telling the story as an adventure without criticism of the lynchers. None of the reports states the race of either man.

Most reports, including the detailed Colorado narrative, say the men were taken from the jail and hanged, but the Sun said the men of Del Norte hunted the Ponds for days, "shot them down," and hanged their bodies. Potter's name also varies: "Sam Potter" in the wire briefs, "Louis Potter" in the Sun, and Samuel Pond in the Colorado narrative, while Judge Bishop's letter calls the pair "Billy Leroy and brother."

bases: Two prisoners were taken from the Del Norte jail by a party or mob and hanged on a tree (A1, A19), reported nationally as lynched by citizens (A2, A3).

Both men were hanged after a party seized the sheriff and the guards and took them from the jail (A19), described as a mob (A1) and as the citizens of Del Norte (A3), in punishment for stage and mail robberies (A14, A11); nothing in the coverage indicates the victims were Black.

The wire briefs (A2, A3, A1), a Lake City judge's letter with a photograph of the bodies (A14) and a separate long narrative (A17, A19) independently report the killing, though the Sun gives a different manner of death (A11).

framing.detail: One-line crime briefs calling the men 'desperadoes', 'notorious' and 'Colorado murderers', with no comment on the mob.
The Denver Republican, via the Elk Mountain Pilot, spoke of the 'tragic end' of the stage robber and retold a judge's joke at his expense.
Judge Bishop's letter, printed in Connecticut, said the execution much relieved the people.
The long narrative headed 'A Colorado Lynching' told the robberies and hanging as an adventure story, with the coroner's exoneration reported without comment.
The Sun presented the brothers as respectable Pennsylvanians turned highwaymen until 'public sentiment precipitated a disaster.'
